findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State and validate what happens when every push exceeds 30 s under the DEFAULT 300 s per-test budget: either fit setup within budget (e.g. a module/test timeout marker sized to the worst case) or explicitly narrow the claimed fix to partially-starved hosts and record that the fully-starved case becomes a timeout.
evidence: Root cause: 'on a starved host every attempt can exceed 30 s; the write still exits 0'

Testing: 'each rebar write spends about 92 s in its retried push and each `_publish` about 32 s, so the shim runs pass `-o timeout=1800` on the pytest command line to lift the 300 s per-test budget for that run only; the module carries no new marker'
AC: 'Both fold cross-clone tests pass under the 32 s push shim (with `-o timeout=1800`) and without it (default budget)' — no AC covers the starved case under the default budget
findings.finding: In the regime the plan's root cause describes ('on a starved host every attempt can exceed 30 s'), the fixed tests still fail. They no longer fail on the setup assertion; they fail on the default 300 s per-test pytest timeout. By the plan's own figures each rebar write spends about 92 s in its retried push and each `_publish` about 32 s. With at least four cross-clone-relevant writes (A create, A comment, B comment, B tag edit) plus their publishes, the setup alone exceeds 300 s. The plan validates the fix only with `-o timeout=1800`, which `make verify` does not pass, and declares that 'the module carries no new marker'. So the acceptance evidence does not show the title's failure mode is resolved under the real `make verify` budget. It shows the failure moves from a setup assertion to a timeout.
findings.location: Testing — 'the shim runs pass `-o timeout=1800` ... the module carries no new marker'; Acceptance Criteria line 1
scenarios: Oversubscribed developer host during `make verify`: every push attempt exceeds 30 s, 4 writes × ~92 s plus publishes exceed 300 s, and the test fails with a pytest Timeout instead of the old 'SETUP:' assertion. This is still a red local verify.
Partially starved host, where only some attempts time out: the fix helps, but the plan does not state that this narrower regime is the one it actually targets.
findings.suggested_fix:
Do one of two things:
1. Add an explicit per-test `@pytest.mark.timeout(...)` to the two tests, sized to the worst-case starved setup (about 4 × 92 s + 4 × 32 s plus the test body), and run the shim acceptance without `-o timeout=1800`.
2. Keep the default budget and rewrite the Root cause/Acceptance to state that the fix targets hosts where the best-effort push gives up within budget, and that a fully starved host now surfaces as a pytest timeout rather than a setup assertion.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State and justify, per publish call site, that no other clone's write can reach origin between the publishing clone's last sync and its `_publish` (so the push is always a fast-forward), or make `_publish` handle a non-fast-forward rejection explicitly.
evidence: "runs a checked `git push -q origin HEAD:tickets` from that clone's tracker (a no-op when the best-effort push already landed)"
"A's later writes are only read by A" — says who reads A's later writes, not whether those writes push to origin before B publishes
The shim makes every push time out, so the reproduction harness never exercises the mixed regime
findings.finding: `_publish` is a plain `git push origin HEAD:tickets`, so it only succeeds if the publishing clone's HEAD is a fast-forward of origin. The plan never states that this invariant holds at every publish point. Two regimes keep it intact: all best-effort pushes land, or all of them time out (the shim regime). The realistic oversubscribed host is a third, mixed regime: some best-effort pushes land and others time out. If a write by one clone (e.g. A's merge or fold) reaches origin while the other clone's write (e.g. B's tag edit) does not, the second clone's HEAD has diverged and `_publish` is rejected as non-fast-forward. That is a new setup failure in exactly the environment the fix targets.
findings.location: Approach — `_publish(tracker)` helper and its call after B's tag edit
scenarios: A's merge or fold best-effort push lands within 30 s; B's tag-edit push times out on all three attempts; B's HEAD lacks A's commit; `_publish(B)` fails with a non-fast-forward rejection.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Address the per-test time budget under slow pushes: state `_publish`'s timeout and either show the worst-case runtime fits in 300 s or justify/adjust the module's budget, with a criterion covering it.
evidence: "each rebar write spends about 92 s in its retried push and each `_publish` about 32 s, so the shim runs pass `-o timeout=1800`"
AC1: "pass under the 32 s push shim (with `-o timeout=1800`) and without it (default budget)"
Context: the failures occur on "oversubscribed hosts" where pushes exceed the 30 s bound
findings.finding: The fix adds wall-clock time per test: each `_publish` is another git push, and every rebar write still spends up to ~92 s in its retried best-effort push. On the oversubscribed hosts where pushes exceed 30 s, the test may now exceed the default 300 s per-test budget and fail with a pytest timeout instead of a setup assertion. The plan lifts the budget only for shim runs, and AC1's default-budget run is taken on a host where pushes do not time out. No criterion shows the fixed tests stay within budget under slow pushes, and `_publish`'s own timeout is unstated.
scenarios: A starved `make verify` run in which two or three writes each burn ~92 s in retried pushes: the test hits the 300 s timeout before reaching its assertions.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify `_publish`'s subprocess timeout (strictly greater than the 32 s shim delay) and that a timeout/non-zero exit fails the test with a SETUP message naming the clone and the write being published.
evidence: Approach: 'runs a checked `git push -q origin HEAD:tickets` from that clone's tracker' — no timeout stated
Testing: 'each `_publish` about 32 s' under the 32 s shim
Root cause: production bounds push at '`_GIT_TIMEOUT = 30` s'
findings.finding: The plan never specifies the timeout bound on the new checked `git push -q origin HEAD:tickets` in `_publish`. Acceptance criterion 1 only holds if that bound is longer than the shim's 32 s delay. If the helper reuses a 30 s bound like production's `_GIT_TIMEOUT`, every `_publish` fails under the shim. If it is unbounded, a hung push on a starved host shows up only as the pytest-level timeout, with no message naming the publish step. The plan's figure 'each `_publish` about 32 s' implies a bound above 32 s but never states it.
findings.location: Approach — 'add a `_publish(tracker)` helper in the test module that runs a checked `git push -q origin HEAD:tickets`'
scenarios: The implementer copies the production 30 s bound into `_publish`: under the 32 s shim every publish times out and AC 1 cannot be met.
No bound on a starved host: a stuck publish consumes the whole 300 s test budget, and the failure reads as a generic pytest timeout rather than 'SETUP: publish of X failed'.
findings.suggested_fix: Give `_publish` an explicit `timeout=` larger than the shim delay (e.g. 120 s). On timeout or non-zero exit, fail with a 'SETUP: could not publish <write> from clone <A|B>' message, mirroring `_sync_from_origin`'s checked style.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Run the cross-clone child writes with REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off (via _run_at env overrides, and for _create's write) so the checked _publish is the only delivery path, or state why the extra ~92 s per starved write can't exceed the 300 s per-test budget.
evidence: Plan Testing: "under the 32 s push shim each rebar write spends about 92 s in its retried push ... so the shim runs pass `-o timeout=1800` ... to lift the 300 s per-test budget"
src/rebar/_store/push.py:55 `_GIT_TIMEOUT = 30`; lines 220-249 retry transport failures within the same write
src/rebar/_io/import_ndjson.py:180 `os.environ["REBAR_SYNC_PUSH"] = "off"` and push.py:173 show REBAR_SYNC_PUSH is the established push-policy override
test module _run_at(..., **env_overrides) already passes extra env through to child_env/subprocess_env
findings.finding: The plan keeps every child write's best-effort push and adds a checked _publish after it. The test still waits through the slow push it is trying to stop depending on. On a host where pushes exceed 30 s, each rebar write spends about 92 s in timed-out retries before _publish runs; the plan's own shim run needs -o timeout=1800 because of this. Each test makes 3 pushing writes on the reported failure path, and the repair test 4 or more (counting fsck --repair-snapshots if it pushes). That can exceed the default 300 s per-test budget on the same oversubscribed hosts that cause the failure. So the fix may replace a setup-assertion failure with a pytest timeout. A structurally different option is better on robustness, run time and determinism. Turn the product push off for these child processes with REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off, an existing knob that import_ndjson.py and the opcert workspace already set. _run_at already accepts **env_overrides. Then make the test's checked _publish the only delivery path, so setup no longer depends on the 30 s bound or its retries at all.
findings.location: Approach / Testing (shim run needs `-o timeout=1800`); tests/integration/test_fold_cross_clone_horizon.py _run_at and the _create call sites
scenarios: On an oversubscribed make-verify host, A's create, A's comment and B's tag edit each time out all 3 push attempts (about 92 s each, about 276 s total). Add the fold, fetch, show and fsck child processes on top and the test exceeds the 300 s default timeout, even though _publish would have delivered the writes correctly.
The repair test adds B's comment push and possibly a push from fsck --repair-snapshots, which pushes it even further past the budget.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass REBAR_SYNC_PUSH="off" in the env for every child-process write in the module. Add it as a default in _run_at, and create the ticket through _run_at (or with the same env) instead of _engine_run. Make the checked `_publish(tracker)` (`git push -q origin HEAD:tickets`) the only delivery step after A's create and comment, B's comment, and B's tag edit. The shim reproduction then no longer needs -o timeout=1800, because no product push runs. Update the helper's docstring to say the production push is turned off so that delivery is a deterministic, checked fixture step.
